statement: In 100 published case reports of health problems after exposure to nitrous oxide (N2O, the gas called laughing gas, used in dentistry, emergency care and anaesthesia and as a propellant for whipped cream, and in recreational settings commonly available in small pressurized cartridges, as the review describes it), pooled in a systematic review of English-language reports found in PubMed from January 1966 to August 2018 (85 publications; Oussalah et al., 2019; institutional funding; no conflicts declared), nitrous oxide exposure is associated with damage to the spinal cord and nerves, mostly alongside signs of vitamin B12 deficiency, with no comparison group. 96 of the 100 had at least one neurological symptom, most often abnormal sensations, numbness or tingling in the limbs (80), unsteady gait or difficulty walking (58) and weakness (43), and also falls or balance problems (24), Lhermitte's sign (15) and ataxia (12); the diagnoses applied by the case authors were most often subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (28), myelopathy (26) and generalized demyelinating polyneuropathy (23), with axonal polyneuropathy in 11 and vitamin B12 deficiency in 14; of the 75 with a spinal MRI reported, 51 showed a T2 signal hyperintensity in the spinal cord. Vitamin B12 was below 150 pmol/L in 58 of the 82 with a value, homocysteine above 15 µmol/L in 28 of 31 and methylmalonic acid above 0.4 µmol/L in 15 of 16, and a combined score placed 28 of 33 as possibly or probably B12-deficient; low haemoglobin was reported in 24 of 43. The patients were 60 men and 40 women, median age 27 (range 0.4 to 76), mostly reported from North America (51) and Western Europe (22); 57 had used nitrous oxide recreationally, 25 received it during surgery, 9 at work and 6 for pain relief, and 76 had regular exposure and 24 a single one. The 24 cases after a single exposure, mostly in surgery in the authors' description, were older (median age 47 against 26) and had lower vitamin B12 (median 74 against 110 pmol/L) than the cases after regular exposure. The amount of exposure was reported for 28 patients and was not associated with any finding. These counts describe published cases, not the risk to people who use nitrous oxide: case reports are written about people who had problems, the review has no count of people exposed, and its authors say it cannot evaluate how often toxicity occurs and that it may be relatively rare given how widely the gas is used. Vitamin B12 coming out on top is partly built into the method: the search required a B12-related term (vitamin B12, cobalamin, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, methionine or folic acid) as well as a nitrous oxide term, so reports that mentioned none of these were not found, and inclusion also required a blood-test value taken before B12 treatment. Other possible causes (diet, absorption problems, alcohol, other drugs, B12 status before exposure) are not among the extraction domains the review describes (two of its ten are not described) and are not reported, the case reports were not appraised, and the review did not test whether B12 treatment prevents or reverses the damage. A self-selected online survey adds a denominator, for self-reported symptoms only (Global Drug Survey 2014; Kaar et al., 2016; no funding; no conflicts declared): of 74,864 respondents, recruited through social media and media partners, 4883 had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months, and of the 4633 of them who answered the question (editors' sum), 200 (4.3%; editors' 95% interval 3.8% to 4.9%) reported persistent numbness or tingling in the arms and legs, lasting days or weeks after use, in the last 12 months, and 74 (1.6%) only earlier. In the same 12 months, of the 4622 to 4653 answering each item (editors' sums), 27.8% reported hallucinations, 24.0% confusion, 5.8% nausea, 4.4% fainting and 1.2% (56) an accidental injury, each as an effect experienced in relation to nitrous oxide use. No symptom was confirmed by examination or tests, 89.2% of these respondents used nitrous oxide with other drugs, there is no comparison group, and the results are unweighted and unadjusted, so the survey cannot show that nitrous oxide caused the symptoms; nor can it tell whether the amount used matters (typical amounts per session were similar in respondents with and without persistent numbness, and the authors' dose–response reading rests on means with no comparison or test). The sample cannot stand for people who use nitrous oxide in general: more than half of all respondents (39,666) went clubbing at least once every three months, and about 30% of the 4883 were UK respondents (editors' calculation), whose last-year use, 20.5%, compares with 2% of 16–59-year-olds in the 2012/13 Crime Survey for England and Wales, as cited by the paper. The review cites the 4.3% as a share of people who use nitrous oxide; it is the share of last-year respondents answering the item who reported the symptom in the last 12 months. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review pooled published reports of 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas), found by searching PubMed for reports that also mentioned vitamin B12 or related blood tests. 57 had used it recreationally and 25 had it during surgery. 96 had nerve symptoms, most often numbness or tingling (80) and trouble walking (58); doctors most often diagnosed damage to the spinal cord or to the nerves outside it, and 51 of 75 spine scans showed a change in the spinal cord. 58 of the 82 people tested had low vitamin B12. The 24 cases after a single exposure, mostly in surgery, were older and had lower B12 than those exposed regularly. Because these are published cases, reported because something went wrong, and the search looked for B12, the review cannot show how often nitrous oxide harms people who use it, at what amounts, or that it caused each case; the authors say such harm may be relatively rare given how widely the gas is used. An online survey that people chose to join gives a rough count: of 4633 people who had used nitrous oxide in the past year and answered, 200 (about 4 in 100) said that in that year they had numbness or tingling in the arms or legs lasting days or weeks, which they put down to the gas. No doctor checked, nearly 9 in 10 had also used it with other drugs, and the survey cannot show that nitrous oxide caused the numbness or how common it is among everyone who uses it.
population: 100 patients described in 85 English-language case reports found in PubMed (January 1966 to August 2018) by a search requiring a nitrous oxide term and a vitamin B12-related term, each with a health outcome after nitrous oxide exposure and a laboratory value before B12 treatment: 60 men and 40 women, median age 27 (range 0.4 to 76), reported mostly from North America (51) and Western Europe (22); exposed recreationally (57), in surgery (25), at work (9), for pain management (6) or otherwise (3); and, in an online survey whose respondents chose to take part (Global Drug Survey 2014, 74,864 respondents; Kaar et al., 2016), the 4883 who had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months (mean age 24.3), of whom 4622 to 4653 answered each harm question
exposure: Nitrous oxide exposure as each case report described it: regular (76; repeated, at least one cartridge a month) or single (24, mostly anaesthetic); amounts reported for few patients and not given here; in the survey, self-reported nitrous oxide use in the last 12 months (amounts not given here)
comparator: None: no group without exposure; within the review, single-exposure cases are compared with regular-exposure cases; the survey's harm questions have no comparison group
outcome: Neurological symptoms, diagnoses applied by the case authors (subacute combined degeneration, myelopathy, polyneuropathy), spinal cord T2 signal hyperintensity on MRI, and laboratory markers of vitamin B12 status (B12, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, combined B12 score) and of anaemia; in the survey, persistent numbness or tingling in the arms and legs lasting days or weeks, and five other effects (hallucinations, confusion, nausea, fainting, accidental injury), each self-reported as experienced in relation to nitrous oxide use, in the last 12 months or earlier
magnitude: Oussalah et al. (2019), 100 patients from 85 publications, no comparison group: at least one neurological symptom 96 (96%, 92.1 to 99.9); paresthesia, numbness or tingling 80 (72.0 to 88.0); unsteady gait or walking difficulty 58 (48.2 to 67.8); weakness 43 (33.1 to 52.9); falls or equilibrium disorders 24; Lhermitte's sign 15; ataxia 12; subacute combined degeneration 28 (19.0 to 37.0); myelopathy 26 (17.3 to 34.7); generalized demyelinating polyneuropathy 23 (14.6 to 31.4); axonal polyneuropathy 11; B12 deficiency diagnosed 14; spinal T2 hyperintensity 51 of 75 (68.0%, 57.2 to 78.8); B12 below 150 pmol/L 58 of 82 (70.7%, 60.7 to 80.8), median 101 pmol/L; homocysteine above 15 µmol/L 28 of 31 (90.3%); methylmalonic acid above 0.4 µmol/L 15 of 16 (93.8%); combined B12 score possibly or probably deficient 28 of 33 (84.8%); low haemoglobin 24 of 43 (55.8%). Single (24) against regular (76) exposure: median age 47 against 26, B12 74 against 110 pmol/L; multivariable odds ratios for a single exposure, age 40 or older 23.95 (3.62 to 158.61), B12 of 74 pmol/L or lower 10.57 (1.70 to 65.90). Exposure amount (28 patients) not associated with any finding. The printed intervals treat the pooled cases as a sample; no frequency among people exposed can be given from the cases. Kaar et al. (2016), Global Drug Survey 2014, self-selected online sample of 74,864, no comparison group: of the 4883 who had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months, reports in the last 12 months among those answering each item (denominators not printed; editors' sums of Table 3, 4622 to 4653): persistent numbness or tingling 200 of 4633 (4.3%; editors' 95% interval 3.8% to 4.9%, sampling error only), earlier only 74 (1.6%), ever 274 (5.9%, editors' calculation); hallucinations 1289 (27.8%); confusion 1108 (24.0%); nausea 267 (5.8%); fainting 205 (4.4%); accidental injury 56 (1.2%). Used with other drugs: 4354 of 4883 (89.2%). Unweighted and unadjusted; no symptom clinically confirmed; no share among people who use nitrous oxide in general can be given.

evidence.locator: 2.1 Data Sources and Searches; 2.2 Study Selection (one paragraph each, p. 2); 2.3 Data Extraction (p. 3); 2.4 Nitrous Oxide Exposure (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: MEDLINE searched through PubMed from January 1966 to August 2018 with a string that required both a nitrous oxide term (protoxide of nitrogen, nitrous oxide, nitrogen protoxide, laughing gas, whippet or whippets) and a term for vitamin B12, cobalamin, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, methionine or folic acid, plus references of retrieved articles; the review cites the MOOSE statement. A case report was retained if it described at least one health outcome related to previous nitrous oxide exposure; excluded were non-English publications, editorials, narrative reviews, congress abstracts, no nitrous oxide exposure, preventive vitamin B12 treatment before exposure, and no reported value of haemoglobin, haematocrit, mean corpuscular volume, serum folate, homocysteine or methylmalonic acid before B12 therapy. Data were extracted on a predefined form said to have 10 domains, of which eight are described (case report, demographics, clinical findings, laboratory values, diagnoses, setting, exposure and spinal MRI; domains 6 and 8 are not described); none of the described domains has an item for alcohol or other drugs, and no such data are reported; disagreements in data extraction were resolved by consensus. Regular exposure was defined as repeated exposure with at least one cartridge a month.

evidence.locator: 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 14, continued on p. 15); 5. Conclusions (p. 15)
evidence.extracted: The authors list as a strength that the meta-analysis of case reports allowed the compilation of unselected patients, thereby reducing the risk of population heterogeneity. As limitations they list the risk of missing data in case reports, laboratory findings not available for all patients (reducing statistical power), thromboembolic events after surgery possibly attributed to the operation, and the exclusion of non-English reports; and they state that, because the meta-analysis rests on single patient reports or small case series, it cannot evaluate how often nitrous oxide toxicity occurs, that such events may be relatively rare as nitrous oxide is widely used, and that large population studies are needed. The Conclusions call for population studies of whether correcting B12 deficiency prevents nitrous oxide toxicity.

evidence.extracted: The abstract states that nitrous oxide can produce severe outcomes, with neurological or haematological disorders in almost all published cases, more than half of them in recreational use, and that the burden related to it is dominated by vitamin B12 deficiency; the Discussion opens by describing a particularly unfavorable risk-benefit ratio for people using it recreationally (no risk or benefit was assessed in the review), gives 96% as the share with neurological or haematological disorders and says three-quarters of patients had low B12 status. The Discussion cites figures from other sources: in the Global Drug Survey 2014 (74,864 participants in 17 countries), lifetime use of nitrous oxide was reported by 38.6% of respondents in the UK and 29.4% in the US (shares of survey respondents, not population figures), and among respondents who had used it, persistent numbness was reported by 4.3% and accidental injury by 1.2%; in the 2016 survey (over 100,000 respondents from over 50 countries), 4% of respondents who had used nitrous oxide reported symptoms of nerve damage. Funding: institutional (i-Site Lorraine University of Excellence, FHU ARRIMAGE, INSERM UMR_S 1256); the authors declare no conflict of interest. Editors' note: 96 is the share with at least one neurological symptom (p. 6), and low B12 was 58 of 82 (70.7%, Table 4, p. 9); the survey figures are second-hand and were not checked against their source.

evidence.extracted: Global Drug Survey 2014: an anonymous online survey that ran for five weeks from mid-November 2013, promoted through social media and media partners (Fairfax Media, MixMag, The Guardian); almost 80,000 people from over 150 countries took part (p. 2), 74,864 respondents are analysed (Table 1, p. 3), and all results are unweighted (p. 3). Use in this sample (Table 1): lifetime 18.8% (95% CI 18.5–19.1), last 12 months 6.5% (6.3–6.7); among UK respondents (n = 7174), 38.6% and 20.5%. The 4883 respondents who had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months (Table 2, p. 4; mean age 24.3, SD 6.7; in the whole sample 39,666 respondents went clubbing at least once every three months, footnote) were all asked whether they had ever experienced six effects in relation to nitrous oxide use, one of them persistent numbness or tingling in arms and legs lasting days and weeks after use (Measures, 2nd paragraph, p. 3); the Results (p. 3) say the majority of them completed these questions. Table 3 (pp. 4–5), in the last 12 months / earlier only / never: persistent numbness 4.3% (200) / 1.6% (74) / 94.1% (4359); hallucinations 27.8% (1289) / 8.5% (392) / 63.7% (2953); confusion 24.0% (1108) / 7.5% (349) / 68.5% (3165); nausea 5.8% (267) / 3.9% (183) / 90.3% (4180); fainting 4.4% (205) / 6.0% (278) / 89.6% (4170); accidental injury 1.2% (56) / 2.0% (91) / 96.8% (4498). The abstract (p. 1) gives 27.8%, 23.9%, 4.3% and 1.2% for hallucinations, confusion, persistent numbness and accidental injury as shares of the 4883 last-year respondents. Use with other drugs: 89.2% (4354) of last-year respondents (Table 2). Editors' calculation: the denominators, not printed, are the row sums of Table 3, from 4622 (confusion) to 4653 (fainting); for persistent numbness 4633, so 200 of 4633 in the last 12 months (95% interval 3.8% to 4.9%, Wilson, sampling error only) and 274 of 4633 (5.9%) ever; about 1471 (30%) of the 4883 last-year respondents were UK respondents (20.5% of 7174).

evidence.locator: Abstract and author affiliations (p. 1); Introduction, 5th paragraph (p. 2); Methods › Sampling strategy (p. 3); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 3, continued on p. 4); Limitations (p. 4); Conclusions (p. 4, continued on p. 5); Table 3, persistent numbness rows for use with other drugs, median days used in the last 30 days and median hits per session (p. 5); Table 4 and its footnote (p. 5); Declaration of Conflicting Interests and Funding (p. 6)
evidence.extracted: The authors describe the recruitment as purposive sampling and say the resulting selection bias may limit how far the findings generalize, while adding that reasonable general-population inferences can be drawn from large, demographically varied purposive samples (Sampling strategy, p. 3). The Limitations (p. 4) say the self-nominating sample may not represent people who use nitrous oxide more widely; that UK respondents were 9% of the sample but 20% of them had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months, so the findings may reflect the UK scene more than a global pattern; and that retrospective self-report, high levels of other drug use, confounding by other substances and recall bias are significant issues; they add that the group has previously shown self-report among early-adopting drug-using groups to be valid. The Introduction (p. 2) cites a last-year prevalence of 2% among 16–59-year-olds, and 6% among 16–24-year-olds, in the 2012/13 Crime Survey for England and Wales, against 20.5% among this survey's UK respondents (Table 1, p. 3). No symptom was examined or tested; the abstract (p. 1) says further work is needed to confirm persistent neurological symptoms in people who use nitrous oxide recreationally. The abstract reads the highest number of hits per session, among respondents reporting accidental injury, as suggesting a dose–response relationship, and the Discussion (p. 4) says heavy use was associated with persistent numbness, which, given nitrous oxide's effect on vitamin B12 metabolism, may represent heavy or dependent users experiencing neuropathy; the support is Table 4 (p. 5): mean hits per session for five of the six effects (no row for confusion), with mean and interval calculated from a Poisson distribution, no values for respondents without the effect, and no test. The table does not say which respondents each mean covers, but its intervals are reproduced as Poisson intervals using the numbers reporting each effect in the last 12 months (editors' calculation; accidents, n = 56: 26.0–28.8), which ignore between-person spread. In Table 3 (p. 5), the median hits per session of respondents reporting persistent numbness in the last 12 months and of those who never did differ little (6, IQR 4–12, against 5, IQR 3–10), and use with other drugs was 89.0% (178) against 88.6% (3,862). The abstract also says the vast majority use nitrous oxide infrequently and their use is not associated with significant harm, and that a subpopulation of heavy users may be using in a dependent pattern; no test compares harm by frequency of use (Table 3 gives only the median days of use in the last 30 days within each effect group, for persistent numbness 0 (IQR 0–2) in the last 12 months against 0 (0–1) never), and no dependence measure is reported. The Conclusions (pp. 4–5) say the prevalence of serious acute harm (accidental injury) appears low and that the findings largely suggest a legal ban is unnecessary. Funding: none; no conflicts declared (p. 6); four of the six authors list Global Drug Survey, which runs the survey, as an affiliation (p. 1).

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_oussalah_2019 (AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low; six critical items not met): published case reports with no comparison group, selected first by being published (reports describe people who had problems) and then by a search that required a vitamin B12-related term and an inclusion rule that required a laboratory value taken before B12 treatment; English only, one database; the case reports were not appraised; other possible causes (diet, absorption, alcohol, other drugs, B12 status before exposure, genetic variants) are not among the described extraction domains and are not reported (one MTHFR deficiency appears among the diagnoses); exposure is as each report described it; single anaesthetic exposures and months of recreational use are pooled. The survey (card sc_kaar_2016, JBI prevalence checklist, high risk of bias; Kaar et al., 2016): self-selected online respondents recruited through social media and media partners, single unvalidated self-report items that respondents linked to nitrous oxide, no examination or tests, 89.2% use with other drugs, no comparison group, unweighted and unadjusted. Very serious for both sources, two levels; one would already reach the floor.

inconsistency.note: Reports from several regions (North America 51, Western Europe 22, China or Taiwan 12, Australia or New Zealand 10 of the 100 patients) describe the same kind of harm; the per-item shares describe the pooled cases and are not compared across studies. The survey's self-reported persistent numbness or tingling points the same way as the case reports; it is a symptom, not diagnosed damage, so the agreement is in kind only.

indirectness.note: Worded for published cases after medical, occupational and recreational exposure (57 of 100 recreational), not for people who use nitrous oxide in general. The survey part is worded for what its respondents reported (self-reported symptoms they linked to nitrous oxide), not for diagnosed nerve damage or for people who use nitrous oxide in general, so it is not indirect as worded.

imprecision.note: The claim rests on the kind of harm described, not on a frequency; the laboratory shares rest on the patients with each value reported (82, 31, 16, 33) and are given with those denominators. The survey's shares are precise for its own respondents (persistent numbness 200 of 4633; editors' 95% interval 3.8% to 4.9%), an interval that reflects sampling error only, not selection, which is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Selection by publication is the main selection problem here and is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

dose_response.note: Exposure amount, reported for 28 patients, was not associated with any finding; in the survey, typical amounts per session were similar in respondents with and without persistent numbness, and the authors' dose–response reading rests on mean amounts among respondents reporting each effect, with no comparison group or test (Kaar et al., 2016); no gradient to rate up.

grade.reasoning: Case reports pooled in a systematic review, and one self-selected online survey of self-reported symptoms: observational, starts low; down two for risk of bias: very low, the floor; never upgraded. Rated as worded, an association in the weakest sense: damage to the spinal cord and nerves, mostly with signs of vitamin B12 deficiency, has been described repeatedly in people after nitrous oxide exposure. The review cannot show that nitrous oxide caused the damage in each case, how often it happens to people who use nitrous oxide, at what exposure, or whether B12 treatment prevents or reverses it, and the share with B12 problems is partly built into a search that required B12-related terms. The survey (Kaar et al., 2016) adds what the case reports lack, a denominator, but a self-selected one and for symptoms respondents themselves linked to nitrous oxide: 200 of the 4633 last-year respondents who answered (4.3%) reported persistent numbness or tingling in the last 12 months. It is independent of the case reports (the review cites it only in its Discussion) and points the same way, but it does not change the rating: its self-selected sample, unconfirmed self-reports, use with other drugs (89.2%) and missing comparison group are the same kind of very serious risk of bias, and the claim is already at the floor; it cannot show causation, frequency among people who use nitrous oxide, or a relation with amount either. The site question is reworded from 'Can nitrous oxide (laughing gas) damage your nerves?' to ask whether it is linked to nerve damage, because a compilation of selected case reports cannot show that it does damage nerves, or how often. Status replicated: the 100 patients come from 85 publications from several regions, describing the same kind of harm; this agreement in kind does not raise the certainty, and the selection makes some agreement inevitable. The survey, independent of the case reports, points the same way for a self-reported symptom. Not used: the abstract's and Discussion's 96% with neurological or haematological disorders (96 is the share with a neurological symptom) and three-quarters with low B12 (58 of 82, 70.7%); the share with at least one haematological abnormality (71.7%), whose denominator is not stated; the authors' description of the cases as unselected, and the Discussion's unfavourable risk-benefit ratio for recreational use, which no data in the review assess; the exposure amounts of the regular-exposure cases, left out so that nothing reads as a threshold (amount, reported for 28 patients, was not associated with any finding); and the review's advice on B12 screening before anaesthesia, which rests on a surgical trial it cites (not read). The survey figure the statement used to give second-hand from the review's Discussion is now read in the survey itself (Kaar et al., 2016): the 4.3% is a last-12-month share among last-year respondents who answered the item (200 of 4633), not a share of people who use nitrous oxide, as the statement and the review had it. Not used from the survey: its statements that most people use nitrous oxide infrequently without significant harm, that some may use it in a dependent pattern and that heavy use was associated with persistent numbness, none of which it tested (harm by frequency of use was described but not tested, dependence was not measured, and the amount comparison has no comparison group or test); its view that a legal ban is unnecessary, which goes beyond its data; its use figures by setting and source; and its harm-reduction tips (Figure 2), which are the authors' advice, not findings. The claim gives no advice on amounts or supplements.
